title: OS-Level AI — Apple Intelligence, Galaxy AI & Windows Copilot+

sections.content:
## What You'll Learn

Every other lesson in this course has covered AI you have to deliberately open — Claude.ai, ChatGPT, Gemini. This lesson covers something different, and arguably more universal: AI that's already baked into the phone in your pocket or the laptop on your desk, running quietly in the background whether or not you ever open a chat window. Apple Intelligence, Samsung Galaxy AI, and Windows Copilot+ are the three major operating-system-level AI layers you're most likely already carrying around. This lesson covers what each one actually does, and — just as importantly — what it means for your privacy settings to matter as much as your choice of chatbot.

## Why OS-Level AI Is Different

A chat AI is something you opt into: you open the app, you type a prompt, you get a response, you close the app. OS-level AI is ambient — it's woven into the operating system itself, watching for opportunities to help without being asked:

- Your phone suggests a reply before you've finished reading a message
- Your laptop can search for 'that PDF about the budget from last month' using AI instead of an exact filename
- Your assistant can act across apps — take something from a photo and put it in a calendar event — without you explicitly invoking an AI tool

This is powerful, but it changes the privacy conversation. When AI is a chat window you open, you decide what to tell it. When AI is built into the OS, it may be processing your messages, screenshots, photos, and location constantly, in the background, based on settings you may never have looked at. That's why this lesson's workshop has you actually go check your own device's settings rather than just reading about the concept.

## Apple Intelligence

Apple's OS-level AI layer, built into iOS, iPadOS, and macOS. At WWDC 2026 (June 8), Apple confirmed a ground-up rebuild of Siri — branded **Siri AI** — under a multi-year deal reportedly worth roughly $1 billion a year to license a custom, large-scale Gemini model from Google for its most demanding capabilities, a genuinely notable move for a company that has historically built everything in-house. This is now a confirmed, shipping architecture rather than a rumor: Siri routes requests through a three-tier system — simple tasks stay fully on-device, moderately complex ones go to Apple's own Private Cloud Compute servers, and the heaviest reasoning tasks route to Google Cloud, with Apple anonymizing and tokenizing each request so that neither Apple staff nor Google can tie it back to an individual user. Siri AI ships as a standalone app with real-time on-screen awareness, rolling out with iOS 27 and the iPhone 18 lineup starting fall 2026, alongside the option to set a third-party assistant like ChatGPT or Claude as your default instead.

**Key features:**
- **Cross-device continuity:** start a task on your iPhone — drafting a message, summarizing a document — and pick it up seamlessly on your Mac or iPad, because Apple Intelligence understands context across your whole device ecosystem, not just one screen.
- **On-device processing by default:** for many tasks (like rewriting text, summarizing notifications, or basic Siri requests), Apple Intelligence processes everything locally on your device, so the data never leaves your phone.
- **Private Cloud Compute for harder requests, Google Cloud for the hardest:** when a task needs more computing power than your device can provide, Apple routes it to Apple's own Private Cloud Compute servers, designed so that even Apple cannot access the data; the heaviest requests now go a step further, to Google's Gemini model running on Apple-controlled, anonymized infrastructure. This is Apple's answer to 'sometimes you need serious cloud compute, but we don't want to compromise the privacy story.'

**Where you'd notice it:** smarter notification summaries, writing tools that rewrite or proofread text system-wide (not just in one app), photo search that understands what's actually in a picture, and — with the Siri AI rebuild — a genuinely conversational assistant that can see your screen, hold a persistent conversation history synced across devices, and act across apps.

## Samsung Galaxy AI

Samsung's answer to OS-level AI, built into Galaxy phones, is now on its third generation — Samsung itself describes the Galaxy S26 series (launched February 2026) as the third generation of Galaxy AI phones, built on Samsung's own Gauss model family plus Gemini integration, and is explicitly positioned around on-device privacy as a direct contrast to AI that depends on constant cloud connectivity.

**Key features:**
- **Circle to Search:** circle, tap, or scribble on literally anything on your screen — a product in a photo, a phrase in an article, a landmark in a video — and Galaxy AI searches for it immediately, without switching apps or copy-pasting.
- **Now Brief:** a daily AI-generated summary of your day — weather, calendar, reminders, health data, and news relevant to you — assembled automatically each morning.
- **On-device emphasis, with a real opt-in control:** Samsung splits processing between on-device features (Call Screening, Now Brief, Scam Detection using an on-device Gemini model) and cloud-dependent ones (Creative Studio image generation, Circle to Search), and a 'Process data only on device' toggle in Galaxy AI settings can block cloud fallback for the features that support it — though Samsung is upfront that not everything can run fully offline yet. Samsung has also been developing a further offline capability, EdgeFusion (built with Korean AI firm Nota), aimed at sub-one-second on-device image generation, though it remains unconfirmed for wide release as of this lesson.

**Where you'd notice it:** live translation during phone calls, AI-powered photo editing (removing objects, adjusting compositions), a Bixby overhaul that now understands natural, conversational requests instead of rigid commands, and note-taking/transcription features baked into Samsung's own apps.

## Windows Copilot+ PCs

Microsoft's approach was different again — and it just shifted significantly. Copilot+ had been a hardware-and-software tier: only PCs with a fast enough on-device AI chip (NPU) qualified as 'Copilot+ PCs' and got AI features baked into Windows itself. At Build 2026 (June), Microsoft reversed that exclusivity: local AI features now target any DirectX 12-capable GPU with at least 4GB of VRAM, not just NPU-equipped Copilot+ hardware. CEO Satya Nadella told developers they now have 'the full scope of GPUs' available for Windows AI features, and Microsoft confirmed that even older cards — an RTX 30-series GPU with 6GB of VRAM qualifies — can run Windows 11's local AI features natively. The reversal came after adoption of dedicated Copilot+ hardware fell short of Microsoft's own projections; NPUs aren't disappearing (they still handle sustained, low-power tasks like live transcription efficiently), but Microsoft has stopped treating the NPU as the exclusive gateway to on-device AI.

**Key features:**
- **Copilot integrated at the OS level:** available directly from the taskbar, able to see and act on what's on your screen, summarize documents, and answer questions without opening a separate app.
- **On-device AI acceleration, now GPU-inclusive:** local AI features (live captions and translation, image generation, and various Copilot capabilities) can now run on a wide range of GPUs, not just an NPU — meaningfully expanding which PCs can use these features locally instead of relying entirely on the cloud.
- **Windows Recall — a genuine privacy tradeoff worth knowing about:** Recall is a feature that continuously takes and indexes screenshots of your own activity on the PC, building a searchable timeline so you can ask 'find that spreadsheet I had open last Tuesday' and get an exact screenshot back. It's a genuinely useful idea — and also a textbook privacy concern, since it means a running, searchable record of everything you've looked at on your own machine exists somewhere. After a significant public backlash when it was first announced, Microsoft delayed Recall, rebuilt it with more opt-in controls and encryption, and revised it more than once — and as of this lesson, Recall specifically (unlike the broader local-AI features above) remains more tied to NPU-equipped Copilot+ hardware and is still not simply on by default the way most OS features are. It's a genuinely useful real-world case study in the tension between convenience and privacy, directly connected to Lesson 1-5 (Privacy & Safety).

## The Throughline: Ambient AI Means Your Settings Are the Decision

With chat AI, the decision that matters is 'which chatbot do I use, and what do I tell it.' With OS-level AI, the decision that matters is buried in your settings menu: what's on, what's processing on-device versus in the cloud, and what's been quietly enabled since your last OS update. Because this AI runs ambiently rather than being invoked, it's easy to never look at those settings at all — which is exactly why this lesson's workshop asks you to go look at your own device, right now, rather than just reading about the concept in the abstract.

You don't need all three ecosystems to benefit from this lesson — most people carry exactly one of these (an iPhone/Mac, a Samsung/Android phone, or a Windows PC). Focus the workshop below on whichever device you actually own.

sections.title: Audit and Adjust Your Own Device's AI Settings
sections.content:
You're going to check what OS-level AI is already doing on your own phone or laptop, and change at least one setting deliberately rather than leaving it on whatever the manufacturer defaulted to.

**Step 1 — Identify which device applies to you** and jump to the matching instructions:

**If you have an iPhone or Mac (Apple Intelligence):**
1. On iPhone: go to **Settings → Apple Intelligence & Siri**. On Mac: **System Settings → Apple Intelligence & Siri**.
2. Note which features are currently enabled (Writing Tools, notification summaries, Siri suggestions, photo features).
3. Look for the section on **Private Cloud Compute** — Apple's documentation (search 'Apple Private Cloud Compute' if it's not directly in settings) explains which requests stay on-device versus which get sent to Apple's servers.
4. Turn off at least one feature you don't actually use (for example, if you never use notification summaries, disable them) — this is your deliberate change.

**If you have a Samsung Galaxy phone (Galaxy AI):**
1. Go to **Settings → Advanced features → Galaxy AI** (naming may vary slightly by model/region).
2. Review which features are active: Circle to Search, Now Brief, AI photo editing, live translate.
3. Check **Settings → Privacy** for what data each AI feature can access, and look specifically for any toggle distinguishing on-device processing from cloud processing.
4. Turn off or reconfigure at least one feature — for example, restrict Now Brief's data sources, or disable a feature that requires cloud processing if you'd prefer on-device only.

**If you have a Windows PC:**
1. Go to **Settings → Privacy & security → Recall & snapshots** (only present on Copilot+ PCs; on other PCs, check **Settings → Privacy & security → Copilot** or the Copilot app's own settings instead).
2. If your PC has Recall, check whether it's currently enabled, and review what controls exist (pause, filter out specific apps/sites, encryption, delete history).
3. If Recall is enabled and you didn't deliberately turn it on, decide whether you want it on — and either disable it or configure app/site exclusions.
4. Also check **Settings → Privacy & security → General** and the Copilot app's own privacy settings for what's being shared.

**Step 2 — Write down, in your own words:**
- What AI features were already active on your device that you didn't consciously turn on?
- Which of them process data on-device, and which send data to the cloud (based on what the settings/documentation actually say — not a guess)?
- What did you change, and why?

**Outcome:** A real, verified change to your own device's AI/privacy configuration — not a hypothetical exercise — plus a clear answer to 'what is my phone or laptop's AI actually allowed to see.'

sections.question: A user wants to understand whether a specific Apple Intelligence feature on their iPhone processes their data on-device or sends it to Apple's servers. What's the most reliable way to find out, based on how Apple Intelligence is actually designed?
options: Assume all Apple Intelligence features are on-device, since Apple markets itself as privacy-focused
Assume all Apple Intelligence features use the cloud, since AI models are too large to run on a phone

Check Apple's own documentation and settings, since Apple Intelligence uses a mix — many features run on-device by default, while more demanding requests are routed to Private Cloud Compute, and which applies depends on the specific feature
It's impossible to know, since Apple does not disclose this information for any feature
sections.explanation: Apple Intelligence deliberately uses a hybrid model: many everyday tasks (rewriting text, basic Siri requests, notification summaries) are processed on-device, while requests that need more computing power are sent to Private Cloud Compute — a system Apple designed specifically so that even Apple cannot access the data, though it does leave the device. Neither blanket assumption (A or B) is accurate, and Apple does publish documentation on Private Cloud Compute's design specifically because this distinction matters to privacy-conscious users. The correct approach is always to check the actual settings and documentation for the specific feature in question, which is exactly what this lesson's workshop has you do.

sections.question: A Windows user upgrades to a new Copilot+ PC and discovers that Recall — the feature that continuously screenshots and indexes their on-screen activity — appears to be available. What is the most accurate description of Recall's current status, based on its actual rollout history?
options: Recall has been enabled by default on all Windows PCs since it was first announced, with no ability to turn it off

Recall was delayed and revised multiple times after privacy backlash, and is still not simply on by default the way most standard OS features are — it ships with more opt-in controls and encryption than originally planned
Recall was permanently cancelled and no longer exists in any form
Recall only exists on Samsung Galaxy phones, not Windows PCs
sections.explanation: Recall is a real, still-evolving feature specific to Copilot+ PCs. After significant public backlash over its privacy implications when first announced, Microsoft delayed the rollout, added encryption and more explicit opt-in controls, and revised the feature more than once before wider release — and it has not simply shipped on-by-default the way a typical feature would. This makes it a genuinely useful teaching example (referenced back to Lesson 1-5, Privacy & Safety) of the real tension between a convenient feature (a searchable record of everything you've done on your PC) and a legitimate privacy concern (that same record existing at all). Options A, C, and D all misstate its actual history and status.

sections.content: **You've completed lesson 19-13.** OS-level AI — Apple Intelligence (now rebuilding Siri on Gemini), Galaxy AI (now on its third generation), and Windows Copilot+ (which just opened local AI features beyond NPU-only hardware) — is likely the AI you interact with the most, even though you never had to open an app for it. You've audited your own device's settings and made at least one deliberate change, which matters more than any single fact in this lesson: as AI becomes ambient rather than something you deliberately open, checking your own settings periodically becomes as important as choosing which chatbot to trust. Lesson 19-19 continues Part 19 with a look at AI smart glasses — the newest ambient AI category, worn rather than carried.
